401k / IRAs are basically a tax deferred wrapper for "investments". they do involve more effort to use in your 30s/40s/50s than a normal account, but the hoops are worth jumping through with a bit of planning. the tradeoff for simplicity and flexibility is being not being able to save more money quickly (and pay less tax) as long as you can comply with the rules.

I think the biggest rule-friendly workaround for the early withdrawal penalties is doing a Roth conversion ladder when your income is low. Basically you pay income tax at 0% or 10% to move money from a traditional IRA to a Roth (which you can take out of the Roth after 5 years). That way money that would have been taxed at 25% or more when you contributed it can effectively be taxed at 0% or close to it. You just need "normal" investments to bridge the 5-year gap.
